newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Speculative sales hit metals prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Speculative sales hit metals prices.

text.p: Industrial metals markets were hit by a wave of speculative selling on Tuesday.

Traders said a decline in copper was not unexpected because the market is suffering from the usual summer slowdown in industrial demand and from rising stocks. But losses in aluminium and zinc were somewhat surprising, given current tight nearby supply.
The traders blamed selling by investment funds.
"It is just the way it is - the funds are prowling around at the moment," one said.
Copper was hard hit, falling to the lowest since December 1996, trading at $2,118 a tonne and showing a loss of nearly eight percent from levels that prevailed only last Thursday.
Key support held at $2,120, however, and by the London close prices had clawed back some lost ground. Last trade was at $2,145, still down $17 a tonne from Monday.
Aluminium was slapped by fund selling as investment interests who bought metal when prices were rising from $1,600 a few weeks ago opted to take profits.
The market managed to hold $1,630, but still ended at $1,634, down $43 from yesterday.
The fall took some by surprise, given a widening of premiums for prompt supply that was seen recently.
London Metal Exchange (LME) authorities monitored the dealings on Tuesday but did seem to see a need to act to stabilise the markets.
Zinc also buckled during the afternoon when copper came under pressure, with liquidation driving the market down to a $1,461 low.
A subsequent bounce helped cut losses, although final trade was at $1,477, still down $15.

In other commodity news, the London-based International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) said it will meet weather experts on September 10 to discuss the effects of an El Nino Pacific current weather pattern on cocoa producing countries.
The ICCO meets on September 9-12 for its council meeting, which includes talks among producing countries.

El Nino can bring dry weather to West African producers, including Ivory Coast, Ghana and Nigeria, but its direct impact on crops is disputed. Local crop analysts say there has been no clear indication that El Nino weather will arrive in West Africa this year, despite effects already seen in other parts of the world, including Indonesia and Ecuador.
